rounds.response:
Run the built‑in troubleshooter first: Settings > Network & Internet > Status > Network troubleshooter and follow any suggested fixes.  
Open Command Prompt as Administrator and run: ipconfig /release then ipconfig /renew then ipconfig /flushdns then netsh winsock reset and netsh int ip reset, then restart the laptop.  
After reboot, open cmd and run ping 8.8.8.8 and ping google.com — if 8.8.8.8 succeeds but google.com fails it’s DNS, if both fail it’s an IP/router issue.  
Also disable any VPN, check Settings > Network & Internet > Proxy is OFF, and temporarily disable third‑party firewall/antivirus.  
If it still fails, try your phone’s hotspot to see if that works and paste here the outputs of ipconfig /all plus the two ping results so I can suggest the next step.

rounds.response:
169.254.x.x means your laptop didn’t get a DHCP lease — first forget the Wi‑Fi (Settings > Network & Internet > Wi‑Fi > Manage known networks > select your SSID > Forget) and reconnect with the password.  
If that doesn’t fix it, open Services (Win+R → services.msc) and verify "DHCP Client" and "WLAN AutoConfig" are Running and set to Automatic; start them if they’re stopped.  
Next, in Device Manager disable then re‑enable the wireless adapter, and if needed uninstall the adapter (do not check “delete driver” unless you want to reinstall manually) and reboot so Windows reinstalls it.  
To determine whether DHCP/router or the adapter is the problem, temporarily assign a manual IP in your router’s subnet (e.g., IP 192.168.1.50, mask 255.255.255.0, gateway 192.168.1.1, DNS 8.8.8.8) and see if you can ping the gateway; success means DHCP was the issue, failure points to the adapter/hardware.  
If it still fails, try your phone’s hotspot and paste the outputs of ipconfig /all and ping 8.8.8.8 here and I’ll suggest the next steps.
